Friendships account for 60% of the difference in happiness between individuals. That’s an extraordinary number, and a reminder that friendship isn’t a nice extra in life. It’s central to human flourishing.

In this week’s episode of Office Hours, I turn to Aristotle and his Nicomachean Ethics to ask an age-old question: what makes a good friend? I share Aristotle’s three types of friendship, and suggest something that might sound counterintuitive: the best of friends are perfectly useless.

Watch the full episode here: https://lnkd.in/eatt_mps

comments.text: We spend so much energy optimizing careers and routines, and the single biggest input to happiness sits quietly outside the spreadsheet.

comments.text: This deeply resonates with me, Dr. Brooks, especially the idea that friendship is foundational to human flourishing rather than simply a pleasant addition to life. I also find it fascinating that you bring Aristotle into this conversation at a time when so many people are experiencing profound disconnection despite being more digitally connected than ever. What you are describing touches something I believe modern society is starving for right now: coherence. Not just productivity or achievement, but relationships, environments, and conversations that create a genuine sense of emotional congruence, steadiness, trust, and belonging in a fragmented world. The idea that the best friendships are “perfectly useless” feels especially powerful because so much of modern interaction has become transactional. There is something deeply regulating and humanizing about relationships that exist simply because two people value one another’s existence.

text:
The last part of a boring task often feels the worst.
Not because it changed, but because your brain notices how much you’ve already endured. Zoom out and the task shrinks.

comments.text:
Daniel Pink this is good stuff, and a topic I studied a lot growing up at Microsoft.

The question I wanted to solve was:
Should you focus on what's before you?
Or focus on what's behind you?

And the nuance comes down to how committed you are to the task.

Zooming out is a great way, too, so you can keep perspective from the balcony view.  And everything in our minds is relative, if we remember what to relate to.

comments.text: This connects to something interesting in Lean thinking. If a task feels brutal at the end, that's information about the process, not just the person's psychology. Toyota's approach would be to ask why the task is structured in a way that creates that experience at all. Can it be broken into smaller cycles? Can the painful part be redistributed? The zoom-out helps the individual cope. But the deeper question is whether the task itself is well-designed — because a process that routinely drains people at the finish line has a structural problem worth solving.

text:
BREAKING NEWS: Andrej Karpathy Joins Anthropic

This was definitely not on my list of predictions.

Andrej is one of the most respected people in AI -- and is particularly known for his ability to explain AI and LLMs to mere mortals like me.

What's even more interesting is what he's going to be working on. Using Claude to accelerate AI research itself.

A lot of the attention in AI goes to apps, agents, benchmarks, and funding rounds. But the deeper leverage may be in improving the research loop: using AI to help build better AI.

The race is very much on.

p.s. I'm going to miss Andrej's work educating the rest of us.

comments.text:
The underrated part of this is what it implies about Anthropic’s bottleneck.

If the constraint were just data or compute, you do not bring in Karpathy. You bring him in when the rate-limiter is research velocity itself: better taste, better evals, better loops for deciding what is actually improving.

For the rest of us, the question is what our version of that move looks like.

Usually it is more boring: the first person you let build the internal eval loop, not the customer-facing AI feature.

Inner loop first.

Tied with Lightfield, ahead of Salesforce, Attio, and Pipedrive on agent-readiness.

Per Appie: “Three things changed everything in the HubSpot API in the past months:

#1. Breeze AI Agents shipped with real developer APIs. Not a chatbot bolt-on

You can orchestrate Breeze across contacts, deals, tickets, and content programmatically. That's a different product than HubSpot was 18 months ago.

#2. Date-based API versioning

The Spring 2026 move to /YYYY-MM/ versioning means agents stop breaking when the platform ships. Sounds boring. Matters enormously when you're shipping autonomous workflows.

#3. Serverless functions in Projects

You can now write logic that runs inside HubSpot's runtime, against HubSpot's data, without standing up your own backend. For B2B + AI teams building on top of CRM data, that's the difference between a 2-week integration and a 2-day one.

The Salesforce vs. HubSpot debate used to be "enterprise scale vs. mid-market ease." For agents, it's a different question now: which platform gets out of your way fastest?

Right now, the data says HubSpot.

(Salesforce is still A- at 85 on the overall — Agentforce 360 is no joke. But HubSpot closed the gap faster than anyone predicted.)”

Did Appy get it right Dharmesh Shah?

comments.text: The Appy ranking framing isn't really about HubSpot leapfrogging Salesforce on the API report card. It's about which contract your API holds with the agent the moment it stops being a developer reading docs over coffee and starts being an autonomous consumer that pays per failed call. McKinsey's 2024 State of AI report showed enterprise adoption stalling at integration, not capability, and that integration surface is exactly where agent-ready contracts diverge from human-ready ones. CRMs that figure out which idempotency, error-shape, and rate-limit defaults their API holds with agents will own the next decade of enterprise lock-in; the ones still measuring success by dashboard MAUs are pricing roadmaps against a buyer who stopped clicking.
